A group of tribal healers from Odisha’s Malkangiri showcasing their traditional medicines at at Samvaad-2026, a tribal convention organised by Tata Steel Foundation in Jamshedpur. | Photo Credit: Special arrangement
As medicinal plants, roots and climbers that sustain traditional tribal healing practices gradually disappear under the combined pressures of climate change and human activities, a group of tribal healers in Odisha has turned to conservation to keep their age-old knowledge alive.
At Makamanali village in Malkangiri district, Nilakantha Krisani, a traditional healer from the Parenga community, tends to medicinal plants on half an acre of land even as he continues to treat villagers for minor ailments. He is joined by septuagenarian Deba Gallori, a Kandh tribal healer who donated the land, and several other healers who have contributed medicinal plants from their respective villages. Their efforts are not aimed at conducting experiments or making profits, but a desperate act at preventing medicinal species from disappearing.
They are not alone. Across Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Jharkhand, tribal healers are taking the initiative to conserve medicinal plants and preserve traditional healing practices.
Sarojini Goyal Paneka, a 43-year-old tribal healer and also post graduate in Botany, says she preserves medicinal plant species and manufacture herbal products with assistance from Chhattisgarh government at Samvaad-2026, a tribal convention organised by Tata Steel Foundation in Jamshedpur. | Photo Credit: Special arrangement
While Sarojini Goyal Paneka, a 43-year-old tribal healer, is fortunate that she has received one acre of land from the Chhattisgarh Forest Department to nurture medicinal plants and manufacture herbal products in Korba district, Sonaram Hansda (40) in Jharkhand laments the lack of awareness among tribal communities about the disappearance of plant species that have sustained their traditional systems of medicine. Though a tribal healer, Ms. Paneka holds a post-graduate degree in botany.
The initiative of preserving plants in their backyard reflects a growing crisis confronting traditional tribal healers across the country. As medicinal plants, roots and climbers become increasingly difficult to find, healers are being forced to venture deeper into forests and travel longer distances to procure them. The dwindling availability of these natural resources is threatening not only their healing practices but also traditional knowledge passed down through generations.
More than 200 tribal healers raised serious concerns over the disappearance of medicinal plants and its impact on their practice at Samvaad-2026, a five-day tribal convention organised by Tata Steel Foundation in Jamshedpur.
A tribal healer from Maharashtra also displays a range of products made from medicinal plant species at Samvaad-2026, a tribal convention organised by Tata Steel Foundation in Jamshedpur. | Photo Credit: Special arrangement
“You may not agree with our line of treatment, but people are benefiting from our medicines. We used to solely depend on medicinal plants found around our villages. Now, many of these plants and roots are no longer available. We have to walk long distances deep into the forests to procure them,” said Mr Gallori.
The healers have called for urgent government intervention to conserve medicinal plant species through dedicated nurseries, propagation programmes and afforestation programmes. They believe that unless steps are taken to protect these plants in their natural habitats and ensure their regeneration, the loss of biodiversity could eventually lead to the erosion of an indigenous healing tradition.
“While conceptualising Samvaad as a platform for tribal communities from across the country to share their knowledge, concerns and challenges threatening their existence, ethnomedicine and traditional healing practices emerged as the biggest talking points. Tribals engaged in extensive discussions on ways to preserve their traditional knowledge,” said Sourav Roy, Chief Executive Officer of Tata Steel Foundation.
Mr. Roy said Samvaad, which began with 40 tribal participants representing 19 States, has grown over the years, with this year’s edition witnessing participation from 165 tribes across 29 States and six Union Territories. In addition, year-round zonal consultations held ahead of the annual convention bring together representatives of around 353 tribes, out of the nearly 700 tribal communities in the country.
Each tribal community has its own traditional healers, known variously as Disari, Kabiraj, Baidya or Ojha. Although the Department of AYUSH has recognised traditional systems of medicine and their practitioners, there is no concerted effort to address the growing scarcity of medicinal plants in forests, which threatens the continuity of these healing practices.
According to the Indian Journal of Natural Products and Resources, nearly half of Malkangiri district is covered by dense semi-evergreen and moist deciduous forests, providing favourable conditions for the luxuriant growth of several valuable medicinal plant species. Researchers have documented 34 plant species traditionally used by local communities to treat 17 ailments. Malkangiri is home to several tribal communities, including the Bonda, Parenga, Didayi, Koya, Paroja, Bhatoda and Kondh. A voluntary organisation has listed 376 tribal healers in Malkangiri in 2009.
A group of woman tribal healers from Tamil Nadu also market their products at Samvaad-2026, a tribal convention organised by Tata Steel Foundation in Jamshedpur. | Photo Credit: Special arrangement
Gangadhar Singh Durba, a tribal healer in Anuppur district of Madhya Pradesh, said despite factors working to derail traditional healing system, the healers have made valiant efforts to make the system alive.
Meanwhile, Ministry of Tribal Affairs and e Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) have joined hand to rope in tribal healers and make them part of larger public health outreach programme.
“Our target is to identify 1 lakh tribal healers and help them diagnose disease through symptoms. We have already set a target to train 1000 master tribal healers and they will, in turn, take 20 healers each under their wings. We have a specific target to tackle tuberoculosis, encephalitis and snakebites. If they come across those cases, they would refer them to nearby hospital facilities, said Sanghamitra Pati, Director of Regional Medical Research Centre, Bhubaneswar, affiliated to Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR).
Dr. Pati said, “we don’t want to interfere with their line of treatment. They can continue traditional treatments. Our goal is to make them champions of public health systems because community trust them.”
